planting.note: Pot divisions into a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix of bark and perlite and hang the container so the long leaves can cascade freely.

directions: This South American epiphyte is grown almost entirely for its extraordinarily long, narrow, strap-shaped leaves that hang like ribbons from a compact crown. Give it bright, filtered light and high humidity as it would receive growing on a tree trunk in cloud forest, and keep the chunky bark-based mix evenly moist but never waterlogged. Its inflorescence is small and inconspicuous, so the pendant foliage is the real display feature, making it best suited to an elevated basket or shelf where the leaves can drape without obstruction. Propagate by dividing offsets at the base once a clump has several crowns.

planting.note: Start dormant tubers or divisions in a gritty, fast-draining mix in spring as the plant breaks dormancy and begins active growth.

directions: Native to shaded rocky outcrops and cliff faces in southern Africa, this small tuberous begonia dies back to a dormant underground tuber during its dry season and resprouts with sharply lobed, succulent leaves when moisture returns. It carries small pink or white flowers in loose clusters during the active growing months and shares the same cliff-dwelling habit as its better-known relatives Begonia dregei and Begonia sutherlandii. Grow it in a shallow pot of mineral-heavy, sharply draining soil, water sparingly while dormant, and increase watering only once new growth appears. Protect it from frost and from prolonged wet soil, which quickly rots the tuber.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring and provide a moss pole or trellis right away, since this begonia climbs by clinging aerial roots like a philodendron.

directions: Unlike the familiar rhizomatous and cane begonias grown for colorful foliage, this tropical American species is a true vine, with glossy succulent heart-shaped leaves on winged stems that climb by producing clinging aerial roots at the nodes. It bears small white to pale pink flowers in loose clusters and is best grown on a moss pole, trellis, or allowed to scramble up a humid greenhouse wall rather than kept as a trailing basket plant. Keep the potting mix consistently moist but well drained, provide warm temperatures and high humidity, and pinch growing tips to encourage branching. Propagate easily from stem cuttings taken below a node.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets from the base of a mature clump in spring and pot into a loose, humus-rich houseplant mix.

directions: This Philippine rainforest-understory species carries lance-shaped leaves marked along the veins with pink or cream speckling, and it stands as one of the key wild parents behind many of the brightly patterned Aglaonema hybrids sold today. It tolerates deep shade better than almost any other foliage houseplant, making it useful for low-light interior spots, though leaf coloration intensifies with a bit more indirect brightness. Keep it warm, away from cold drafts, and water only once the top inch of soil has dried, since soggy roots are its main vulnerability. Propagate by dividing the basal offsets a mature plant produces over time.
sources: University of Florida IFAS foliage plant notes

planting.note: Root a stem cutting with at least one node in moist sphagnum in spring, then pot up and provide a support for its climbing habit.

directions: Native to the understory forests of northern South America and Trinidad, this climbing hemiepiphyte is named for the rust-copper tone of its emerging leaves and petioles, which deepen to glossy green as they mature. Its elongated, ovate leaf blades are produced along a vining stem that climbs readily up a moss pole or nearby support when given something to grip. Provide warm temperatures, high humidity, and bright indirect light, and let the chunky, well-draining aroid mix dry slightly between waterings to avoid root rot. Propagate from stem cuttings that include at least one node and a few aerial roots.
